<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate identification of transition states (TSs) is fundamental to computational chemistry. Modern reaction-discovery efforts increasingly rely on curating and completing large reaction datasets, where even a small fraction of TS-search failures can leave key pathways unresolved and bias the resulting reaction network. Here, we introduce an adaptive evolutionary framework for TS search workflows that prioritizes completion of a target dataset over global algorithmic robustness. The framework iteratively focuses on reactions for which no validated TS has been found and dynamically modifies the workflow to search the remaining TSs. Rather than converging toward a single universally optimal TS search workflow, the framework generates a sequence of specialized workflow variants that collectively increase TS coverage across the dataset. Applied to the Transition1X benchmark (over 10,000 reactions), this adaptive evolution improves a state-of-the-art TS-search workflow to achieve a >80% success rate of TS-finding with rigorous validation via eigenvector analysis and reaction path endpoint confirmation. More broadly, these results suggest that adaptive, LLM-driven evolutionary workflow optimization provides a transferable strategy for improving validated TS coverage in large-scale, failure-prone scientific workflows.</jats:p>
title: Evolving transition-state search with agentic large language models

items.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate identification of transition states (TSs) is fundamental to computational chemistry. Modern reaction-discovery efforts increasingly rely on refining large reaction datasets, where even a small fraction of TS-search failures can leave key pathways unresolved and bias the resulting reaction network. Here, we introduce an adaptive evolutionary framework for TS search workflows that prioritizes completion of a target dataset over global algorithmic robustness. The framework iteratively focuses on reactions for which no validated TS has been found and dynamically modifies the workflow to search the remaining TSs. Rather than converging toward a single universally optimal TS search workflow, the framework generates a sequence of specialized workflow variants that collectively solve the dataset. Applied to the Transition1X benchmark (over 10,000 reactions), this adaptive evolution refines a state-of-the-art TS-search workflow to achieve a 99.96% TS localization success rate. More broadly, these results suggest that adaptive, LLM-driven evolutionary workflow optimization provides a transferable strategy for achieving near-complete coverage in large-scale, failure-prone scientific workflows.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Networking industry is changing fast, with the complexity growing with the implementation of cloud computing, the Internet of things, and multi-vendor environments (Oswalt et al., 2023). Manual and semiautomated approaches to network management lack the capability to support the rigorous demands of real-time decision-making, scalability and responsiveness to dynamic situations. In this paper, a conference proposal has been presented, and it suggests a holistic framework that incorporates the Model Context Protocol (MCP), large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and autonomous AI agents, as a means of network management. Human-in-the-loop controls are provided in the framework to maintain compliance with regulatory and organizational requirements.     We created an ecosystem which integrates specialized  AI agents - Routing, Optimization, Implementation,  Monitoring, and Notification - coordinated through n8n  and anchored through Retrieval-Augmented Generation  (RAG) to provide factual accuracy in accordance with  enterprise network spaces. The system converts  operator intent in managing networks into verified  network settings, performs proactive optimization and  maintains audit trails, thus ensuring that enterprise  networks perform optimally.  This study adds value to the research area by showing  how machine-learning and LLM based techniques can be  practically applied to end-to-end network operations as  the blueprint to reliable autonomous networking. In  addition, this paper stresses that there are certain  computing requirements required to implement and  maintain an ecosystem of this kind.</jats:p>
title: A Design Science Approach for Agentic AI in Network Engineering: Autonomous Network Management Using AI Agents, Large Language Models (LLM) And Model Context Protocol (MCP) Mechanisms

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have undergone a dramatic transformation from static text-completion engines to dynamic, tool-wielding autonomous agents capable of planning, reasoning, and executing multi-step tasks in real-world environments. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the architectural principles, training paradigms, and emergent capabilities that underpin modern LLMs such as GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro. We examine the progression from transformer-based language models toward agentic AI systems that integrate memory modules, external tools, and multi-agent coordination frameworks. Key topics include the Retrieval- Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigm, chain-of- thought and tree-of thought prompting strategies, the ReAct framework, and multi-agent orchestration platforms such as AutoGen and CrewAI. We further present a structured experimental comparison of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and ReAct prompting paradigms across 120 standardized tasks spanning multi-step question answering, logical inference, and knowledge-retrieval scenarios, provide in reproducible methodology and statistical analysis. We also discuss open challenges in safety, alignment, hallucination mitigation, and computational costs associated with large-scale deployment. Our analysis reveals that while agentic AI demonstrates remarkable potential in software engineering, scientific research, and enterprise automation, significant hurdles in reliability, explainability, and ethical governance must be addressed before wide- scale deployment can be responsibly achieved.</jats:p>
title: Large Language Models and Agentic AI: How Modern AI Systems Are Evolving Into Autonomous Agents

title: Agentic and Less-Agentic Orientations in TESOL Student Teachers’ Motivation

items.abstract: Learning management systems have become indispensable institutional infrastructure, but their capability repertoires remain largely fixed at design time. Next-generation digital learning environment and adaptive-learning approaches improve modularity, interoperability and runtime personalisation, yet they usually vary content, sequence or feedback within a predefined set of functions. Agentic artificial intelligence and self-evolving computing create a different possibility: a learning environment able not only to select among existing pedagogical actions but also to compose, test, deploy and retire bounded capabilities in response to emerging learner need. This conceptual article develops that possibility through a theory-synthesis and model-building approach spanning learning management systems, adaptive learning, self-regulated learning, intelligent tutoring, agentic AI, self-adaptive software, organic computing and responsible AI. It proposes the Self-Evolving Agentic Learning System (SEALS), defined as an institutionally governed digital learning system that senses changing learning conditions, reasons over pedagogical goals and constraints, composes or develops capabilities, evaluates their effects and selectively retains, modifies or retires them. The framework makes three theoretical moves. First, it introduces capability personalisation, in which functions, interfaces and workflows can adapt rather than only the content delivered through fixed functions. Second, it distinguishes adaptation within a known operational domain from evolution of the capability boundary itself. Third, it treats organicity as bounded, evidence-bearing and reversible evolution rather than unrestricted self-modification. SEALS combines six interacting planes, four nested evolution loops, a stable core and adaptive periphery, a capability graph, a bounded capability-evolution lifecycle and a risk-tiered autonomy ladder. Seven propositions specify how pedagogical quality, learner agency, assurance, architectural boundaries, contestability and long-term independence condition educational value. The paper contributes a vocabulary, system architecture and research programme for studying e-learning environments whose capacity to change is itself designed, governed and evaluated in educational terms.
title: Beyond the Static LMS: A Conceptual Framework for Self-Evolving Agentic E-Learning Systems
